findings.message: `collect_indexes_recursive` and `write_indexes_recursive` never check `config.readme.max_depth`. They recurse unboundedly into all subdirectories, while `validate_readmes` (via WalkDir) does respect `max_depth`. A project configured with `max_depth = 1` will have validation limited to one level, but `aps run docs index --write` will scan and overwrite README files arbitrarily deep. These two behaviours are inconsistent and the index commands can touch files the user never intended.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `collect_indexes_recursive` and `write_indexes_recursive` in lib.rs never consult `config.readme.max_depth`. They recurse unconditionally into all non-excluded, non-hidden subdirectories. `validate_readmes` in readme.rs does respect `max_depth` via WalkDir's `max_depth` setting. The inconsistency is real and code-specific.
findings.severity_justification: A user who sets `max_depth` to limit scope will see validation behave differently from `index --write`, which will silently overwrite README files deeper than intended. This is a behavioral inconsistency that can cause unexpected file mutations.
findings.category_justification: The index write/generate functions do not honor a user-configured depth constraint, contradicting the configured behavior of the validator they are paired with.

findings.message: `update_readme_index` always calls `std::fs::write` even when the newly generated content is identical to what is already on disk. There is no early-exit comparison between `new_content` and the original `content`. In CI workflows that run `aps run docs index --write` and then check for dirty files, every run will mark every README as modified even when nothing actually changed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The function does unconditionally write, but the claim that 'every run will mark every README as modified' in CI git checks is incorrect. Git compares file content, not mtime; writing identical bytes back produces no git diff. The only real issue is that the `count` return value and progress message are inflated (counting files even when content was unchanged), which is cosmetic. The specific CI concern stated in the finding is inaccurate.
findings.severity_justification: The unconditional write is a minor inefficiency (extra I/O, inflated count message) but does not cause the stated CI problem since git detects no change when bytes are identical.
findings.category_justification: The finding targets a behavioral issue — unnecessary writes — but the specific harm claimed (CI false positives) doesn't hold.

findings.message: Relative `--config` paths are resolved against `target` (the docs validation path), not the current working directory or `repo_root`. When the user runs `aps run docs validate src --config .apss/config.toml`, `target` becomes `repo_root/src`, so the resolved config path is `repo_root/src/.apss/config.toml` instead of `repo_root/.apss/config.toml`. The same bug exists in the `index` command. The comment even says 'Resolve relative --config paths against the target directory', which is the wrong anchor — the standard places config at `.apss/config.toml` relative to the repo root, not the docs target.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified in both the validate and index commands: relative `--config` paths are resolved with `target.join(cfg)` where `target` is the positional docs path, not `repo_root`. The standard specifies config at `.apss/config.toml` relative to repo root. The comment even acknowledges this by saying 'against the target directory', confirming the wrong anchor is intentional but incorrect.
findings.severity_justification: Users who pass a relative `--config` path with a non-root target path will silently fail to load their config (or load the wrong one), causing validation to use defaults instead of configured settings. Not data-loss but causes silent misconfiguration.
findings.category_justification: The path resolution logic produces the wrong absolute path for a common usage pattern, causing the wrong config file to be loaded.

findings.message: Dead and superseded ADR reference warnings are emitted once per occurrence in a file, with no deduplication. If a source file mentions `ADR-999-ghost` five times, five separate `ADR01-009` warnings are produced for the same file and the same dead reference. In practice this makes the output very noisy for files that consistently reference an ADR across many call sites. A `HashSet` of already-warned `(path, adr_ref)` pairs would fix this.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `extract_adr_references` returns all regex matches including duplicates, and the for loop pushes a diagnostic for every element without any deduplication check on `(path, adr_ref)` pairs. Multiple mentions of the same dead ADR in a file produce multiple identical warnings.
findings.severity_justification: The output becomes noisy when a file references the same ADR multiple times, but functionality is not broken — the issue is just extra diagnostic noise. Easy to workaround by fixing the reference.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about output quality/readability of diagnostics rather than incorrect behavior — the warnings are technically correct, just redundant.

findings.message: `validate_adr_references` performs an unbounded full-repository walk, reading every file whose extension is in `SOURCE_EXTENSIONS` (which includes `.md`, `.rs`, `.py`, `.ts`, `.json`, `.toml`, etc.) into memory with `read_to_string`. There is no file-size guard, no concurrency limit, and no caching. On a large monorepo this runs O(total source file bytes) synchronously on every `aps run docs validate` call. A binary file accidentally named with a scanned extension (e.g., a large `.json` data dump) will be read entirely into memory.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the function walks the entire repo and calls `read_to_string` on every file matching `SOURCE_EXTENSIONS` with no size guard. The claim is factually accurate — large `.json` files or generated data files would be read entirely into memory. The `exclude_dirs` config partially mitigates this but doesn't guard against large individual files.
findings.severity_justification: This is a developer/CI tool, not a server. Typical source repos handle this fine with proper `exclude_dirs` config. The risk of a large binary-named-as-.json causing OOM is real but unlikely in practice and already partially mitigated by exclusion lists.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about unnecessary memory consumption from reading large files in full, an O(total source bytes) operation with no size guard.

findings.message:
The `or_else(|| after_open.find("
---"))` branch is dead code. The substring `"
---"` always contains `"
---"`, so `find("
---")` will always find a match first when CRLF line endings are present. The `close_pos` returned on a CRLF file lands at the `
` character, so `after_open[..close_pos]` includes the trailing `` of the YAML block. This `` is stripped by the subsequent `.trim()` call, so the result happens to be correct — but the design is misleading: the `
` path is never exercised, test coverage does not catch this, and the comment 'handle both LF and CRLF' is false.
findings.tp_fp_justification:
Verified: `find("
---")` is a substring search, and `"
---"` contains `"
---"`, so the `or_else` branch can never execute. CRLF is incidentally handled by `.trim()` stripping the trailing ``. The comment claims explicit CRLF support that doesn't actually function as described, and the `or_else` branch is dead code.
findings.severity_justification: The end result is functionally correct due to `.trim()`, so there is no actual bug. The issue is a misleading comment and dead code that could confuse future maintainers or lead them to believe explicit CRLF handling exists when it doesn't.
findings.category_justification: Dead code with a misleading comment — the `or_else` branch and the 'handle both LF and CRLF' comment are both incorrect but don't cause bugs.

findings.message: Errors from `index::validate_index` (e.g., failure to read the directory during `generate_index`) are silently swallowed with `Err(_) => { // Non-fatal: index validation failed, skip }`. This means that if `std::fs::read_dir` fails mid-validation — e.g., due to a permissions issue on a docs subdirectory — neither `MISSING_INDEX` nor `STALE_INDEX` is reported for that directory and the validator exits cleanly, giving a false 'passed' result.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the `Err(_)` branch at line 148 silently discards any `IndexError` from `validate_index` (which wraps `read_dir` failures). If the directory scan fails, the validator emits no diagnostic and reports clean — a false negative.
findings.severity_justification: In practice, `read_dir` failing on a directory already enumerated by WalkDir in the same run is rare. The false-clean scenario requires an unusual permission setup or race condition. The impact is a missed warning, not a crash or data corruption.
findings.category_justification: Silently swallowing I/O errors causes the validator to report a false-clean result when it should either surface the error or emit a diagnostic, undermining the tool's reliability as a linter.

findings.message: The quote-stripping logic checks `value.starts_with('"') && value.ends_with('"')` without requiring the string to be at least two characters long. A front matter value that is exactly a single double-quote character (`"`) satisfies both conditions, and `value[1..value.len()-1]` degenerates to `value[1..1]`, producing an empty string rather than preserving the literal quote. The same applies to a single single-quote. While unusual YAML, it silently discards the value rather than reporting a parse error.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code pattern is genuinely missing a length check: `starts_with` and `ends_with` match for a single-char string, and the subsequent slice `value[1..0]` (start > end) would panic in Rust at runtime. The underlying code issue is real. The finding misstates the symptom ('empty string' vs actual panic), but the root cause identification and suggested fix are correct.
findings.severity_justification: Requires a YAML front matter value to be exactly a single quote character (e.g., `key: "`), which is extremely unusual in practice. The panic would be a hard failure on that specific malformed input, but normal/valid YAML front matter is unaffected.
findings.category_justification: A logic bug in the quote-stripping code that leads to a runtime panic on an unusual (but possible) input.

findings.message: `valid_stems.is_empty()` early exit in `validate_adr_references` is intended to skip scanning when there are no ADRs, but `adr_stems(adr_files)` always includes stems for structural files (`CLAUDE`, `AGENTS`, `README`) present in the ADR directory. The set is therefore never empty when the ADR directory exists and contains those files, so the guard never fires even when there are zero real ADR documents. Scanning will proceed over the entire repository unnecessarily.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `collect_adr_files` returns all `.md` files including structural ones, and `adr_stems` strips `.md` without filtering them. The unit test even acknowledges this with 'structural files still get stemmed, that's fine'. With only structural files in the ADR dir, `valid_stems` is non-empty so the guard doesn't fire, causing an unnecessary full repo scan.
findings.severity_justification: The consequence is primarily a performance concern (unnecessary repo scan when no real ADRs exist). There's also a secondary issue where any ADR references in source code would be flagged as dead, but this is mostly a new-project scenario unlikely to have source ADR references anyway.
findings.category_justification: The early-exit guard logic is incorrect — it does not serve its intended purpose of skipping the repo scan when no real ADRs exist.

findings.message: When `--config` is provided to `aps run docs validate`, the `DocValidator` is constructed with `&target` as its repo root, but `AdrValidator::with_config` is also called with `&target`. Both validators will therefore treat `target` (the docs path argument) as the repository root when searching for ADR directories and root-level context files. If the user passes a sub-path (e.g., `aps run docs validate docs --config /abs/path/config.toml`), the ADR validator will look for `docs/docs/adrs/` and the context validator will look for `docs/CLAUDE.md`, both of which are wrong.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: both `DocValidator::with_config(&target, ...)` and `AdrValidator::with_config(&target, ...)` use `target` (the positional path argument) as repo root. `resolve_docs_root` and `resolve_adr_dir` then join config paths onto this, causing double-nesting when a sub-path is passed (e.g., `target = repo_root/docs` leads to looking for `repo_root/docs/docs/adrs/`). The same issue exists in the non-`--config` load path.
findings.severity_justification: The validators produce wrong paths for ADR directories, docs roots, and root context files whenever a non-root target is passed. Users who follow the documented `aps run docs validate [path]` interface expecting `path` to be a docs sub-directory would get incorrect results.
findings.category_justification: Wrong path resolution leads validators to search incorrect filesystem locations, producing false negatives or errors.

findings.message: The `.unwrap_or(cfg)` fallback in `load_docs_config` can lead to an incorrect file path being used if `cfg_path.to_str()` returns `None`. `cfg_path` is a `PathBuf`, so `to_str()` will only fail if it contains non-UTF-8 characters. In that unlikely but possible scenario, `unwrap_or` would use the original `cfg` path, which could be relative and resolved against the wrong directory. This might cause the application to read the wrong configuration file or fail to find it. Instead of falling back, it would be safer to propagate an error or handle the invalid path explicitly.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The code pattern is real: `cfg_path.to_str().unwrap_or(cfg)` silently falls back to the original relative `cfg` string if `PathBuf::to_str()` returns None. The fallback would use an unresolved relative path, potentially reading the wrong config file or failing silently. The concern is factually correct and code-specific.
findings.severity_justification: Non-UTF-8 path components on a `PathBuf` constructed entirely from `&str` sources plus `repo_root` is extremely improbable on mainstream platforms. This is a theoretical correctness issue with negligible real-world impact.
findings.category_justification: The fallback logic silently degrades to an incorrect path rather than propagating an error, which is a reliability concern in error handling.

findings.message: The `parse_simple_yaml` function does not correctly handle values that contain a colon, such as URLs. The line is split only on the first colon found, causing any subsequent characters, including parts of the URL, to be truncated. For a line like `url: http://example.com`, the value will be parsed as just `http`. This will lead to incorrect metadata being extracted from frontmatter.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The analysis is wrong. `line.find(':')` finds the first colon — the key-value separator (`url:`). Everything after that position becomes the value: `line[colon_pos+1..].trim()` = `"http://example.com"`. The URL's internal colon is not a split point. The value is correctly preserved for URL-containing front matter.
findings.severity_justification: The described bug does not exist; the parsing is correct for URLs in YAML values.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about incorrect parsing behavior, which would be a correctness issue if real.

findings.message: The custom fields logic in `render_index_table` is incomplete and will render empty values for any custom field that is not `description`. It filters out the `name` field, but then inside the loop over entries, it only checks for `description` and provides `""` for everything else. This means if the config is `frontmatter_fields = ["name", "status"]`, the 'Status' column in the generated table will always be empty.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `IndexEntry` stores only `filename`, `name`, and `description`. The custom-fields rendering loop at lines 124-131 only handles `description` by name; all other fields fall through to `""`. Config `frontmatter_fields = ["name", "status"]` would produce a Status column that's always empty.
findings.severity_justification: The config option `frontmatter_fields` is documented and user-facing. Users who configure custom fields beyond `description` will silently get empty columns in generated indexes — the feature appears to work but produces wrong output with no error.
findings.category_justification: The custom fields rendering logic is incomplete, silently producing empty values for any configured field other than `description`.

findings.message: When the `docs_root` directory does not exist, a diagnostic is added with `MISSING_README` as the error code. This is misleading, as the root directory itself is missing, not just a `README.md` file within it. Using a more accurate error code, or creating a new one, would provide clearer feedback to the user about the actual problem.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `MISSING_README` is emitted at line 24 when the entire docs root directory is missing, not just a README.md. The error code semantically means 'directory missing README.md' per its doc comment, but is reused for the distinct case of 'docs root itself doesn't exist'. The message text is correct but the code is wrong.
findings.severity_justification: The human-readable message is accurate ('Docs root directory not found'), so users understand the problem. The misuse only affects tooling/CI that parses error codes programmatically. A cosmetic/categorization issue with no functional impact.
findings.category_justification: Reusing the wrong error code for a distinct error condition reduces diagnostic precision and clarity for consumers of the error codes.

findings.message: The file walker in `validate_adr_references` can process the same directory multiple times if symbolic links create cycles. The `WalkDir` constructor is not configured to detect loops, which can lead to infinite loops and a hang for projects with recursive symlinks in their structure.
findings.tp_fp_justification: WalkDir defaults to `follow_links(false)`, meaning symlinks are listed as entries but their targets are not traversed. Symlink cycles can only cause infinite loops when `follow_links(true)` is used. The code never sets `follow_links(true)`, so the claimed infinite loop scenario cannot occur. The parent standard's explicit `.follow_links(false)` in readme.rs merely makes the default explicit.
findings.severity_justification: The described issue doesn't exist given WalkDir's default behavior.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about potential infinite loops during file traversal.

findings.message: The `validate_adr_references` function does not check if the content of a file is valid UTF-8 before passing it to `extract_adr_references`, which expects a `&str`. If a scanned file (e.g., a binary file with a `.json` or `.sh` extension) contains non-UTF-8 byte sequences, `std::fs::read_to_string` will fail, and the file will be silently skipped. This could result in dead ADR references being missed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While `read_to_string` silently skips non-UTF-8 files, the claimed consequence (missed ADR references) is self-contradictory: ADR references are ASCII text patterns, and any file containing them is valid UTF-8 at minimum. A file failing UTF-8 decoding is a binary file and won't contain searchable ADR text references. The silent skip is the correct behavior for binary files accidentally sharing a scanned extension.
findings.severity_justification: Even if the concern were valid, it would only affect an extremely unusual scenario: a source file with non-UTF-8 bytes that also contains ADR reference patterns.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about silent error handling during file I/O in a scanning operation.

findings.message: The `resolve_adr_dir` function directly concatenates paths without verifying if the resulting path fits a valid directory structure. This could lead to incorrect behavior if the directory configuration contains unexpected values.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is too vague and generic — it says 'unexpected values' could cause 'incorrect behavior' without specifying what those values are or what failure actually results. The real concern (absolute paths in config causing `Path::join` to escape `repo_root`) exists but isn't stated. As written, the same comment could be copy-pasted to any code that builds paths from config values. It doesn't identify a concrete issue specific to this code.
findings.severity_justification: Even if the path-replacement concern were stated explicitly, config values come from the user's own `.apss/config.toml` in their own repo — there's no security boundary being crossed.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns path construction validity.

findings.message: The index validation logic does not check for circular references or recursive directory traversal, potentially causing the application to hang or crash for specific unusual directory structures.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The referenced lines are string-scanning code (`find_index_section`) with no directory traversal. `validate_index` calls `generate_index` which uses non-recursive `read_dir`. There is no circular reference risk in the index validation logic. The finding is generic and misapplied to code that doesn't perform recursive directory traversal.
findings.severity_justification: The claimed issue doesn't exist in the referenced code.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns potential infinite loops/hangs during traversal.

findings.message: The `FrontMatterError` enum does not provide enough diagnostic details about input-specific issues (e.g., malformed YAML keys or values), which can make debugging parsing errors more difficult for users.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is a generic best-practice suggestion about error type expressiveness. The `FrontMatterError` enum has two variants (`Unclosed` and `IoError`) matching the two actual failure modes of `parse_frontmatter` — the parser never returns an error for malformed keys/values, it just silently skips them. There are no unreported parse errors to surface. The finding restates a general principle ('more error variants = better debugging') without identifying a specific case where a user would be confused by the current error output.
findings.severity_justification: No concrete debugging scenario is broken — the parser already surfaces the only two error conditions it can produce.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about error type expressiveness and developer experience, not a behavioral bug.

findings.message: The `doc_config` field of the `DocValidator` structure does not validate the fields of the configuration prior to proceeding with validation operations, potentially leading to unexpected failures downstream.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is a generic 'validate your inputs at construction time' suggestion with no specific failure mode identified. The finding doesn't name which config fields are invalid, what values would cause downstream failures, or what those failures would look like. All config fields have `#[serde(default)]` with sensible defaults, and the only field with domain-specific validation already handled downstream is `naming_pattern` (validated by `Regex::new` in `validate_naming` with a proper `ADR01-006` error). The finding is a boilerplate observation about defensive programming.
findings.severity_justification: No concrete failure scenario is identified. The config has sensible defaults for all fields and downstream code handles invalid values where they matter.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about validation at construction time vs. use time — a design preference, not a concrete bug.

findings.message: The test `test_invalid_toml_returns_error` only verifies that an invalid configuration returns an error but does not assert the type of `ConfigError` received, reducing its utility in ensuring robust error differentiation.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is factually correct that the test only checks `is_err()` without asserting the `ConfigError` variant. However, this is a generic test quality observation ('assert error variants, not just is_err') that could be copy-pasted to any test in any codebase. It doesn't identify a concrete scenario where the current test would pass while hiding a real bug — invalid TOML reliably produces `ParseError` regardless.
findings.severity_justification: The test correctly catches the error condition. The lack of variant assertion is a minor precision gap with no realistic bug-hiding consequence.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about test assertion granularity for error cases.

findings.message: Error handling for read failures in the `validate_docs_reference` function is minimal—it simply returns silently, which could cause missing references to go unnoticed during validations.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `validate_docs_reference` is only called when the file is confirmed to exist, so a silent `read_to_string` failure in that function produces a false-clean result — the `MISSING_DOCS_REFERENCE` warning is never emitted even though the file's content is unknown.
findings.severity_justification: The `MISSING_DOCS_REFERENCE` check is a warning-level diagnostic. Requires a file to exist but be unreadable (race condition or unusual permissions), which is rare in practice. Impact is a missed warning, not a crash or data loss.
findings.category_justification: Silent error handling causes the validator to produce a false-clean result when an I/O failure occurs mid-validation.

findings.message: The `write_indexes_recursive` function assumes without validation that every target directory can be written to, which may fail silently for readonly directories and lead to partial writes.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Write failures are not silent. `update_readme_index` returns `IndexError::WriteError` on `fs::write` failure, propagated via `?` through `write_indexes_recursive` → `write_indexes` → `dispatch_docs`, where it is caught and reported as an error with `ExitCode::FAILURE`. The finding incorrectly characterizes a correctly-propagated error as a silent failure.
findings.severity_justification: No actual silent failure exists; errors propagate correctly.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns write failure handling in a file-writing operation.

findings.message: The clause to skip hidden folders when validating READMEs may not work on all operating systems, leading to unintended directories being processed.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The `starts_with('.')` check for hidden/conventional directories is a developer toolchain convention that works identically on all platforms for dot-prefixed directories like `.git`, `.github`, `.apss`. The finding is vague ('may not work on all operating systems') without specifying which OS, which directory name would fail, or what the actual failure mode is. This is a generic portability concern that doesn't identify a concrete code issue.
findings.severity_justification: No concrete failure scenario is identified. Dot-prefix directories are handled consistently on all platforms.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns cross-platform behavior of directory name filtering.

findings.message: The default directory values (like `docs.root` and `docs.readme.exclude_dirs`) are hardcoded in the codebase but are not validated against filesystem constraints at startup, risking runtime errors.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is a generic 'validate config at startup' suggestion with no specific failure identified. The default values ('docs', 'adrs', 'node_modules', '.git', etc.) are all valid directory name strings that cannot violate filesystem constraints. The validator already handles the case where configured paths don't exist (e.g., MISSING_README when docs root is absent). The finding doesn't identify what 'filesystem constraints' the defaults violate or what 'runtime error' would result — it's boilerplate input-validation advice that doesn't apply to these specific default values.
findings.severity_justification: The default values are simple valid directory names. No runtime error can result from them failing filesystem constraints.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns runtime errors from unvalidated config values.

findings.message: The `validate` method of `DocValidator` does not short-circuit for disabled submodules (e.g., ADR validation), leading to unnecessary processing and log noise.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is factually wrong. `validate_readmes` checks `readme_config.enabled` and returns early if false; `validate_root_context` checks `root_config.enabled` and returns early if false; `DocValidator::validate` checks `docs_config.enabled` and returns early. ADR validation is not part of `DocValidator` — it's a separate `AdrValidator`. All submodules already have their own enabled short-circuits.
findings.severity_justification: The described issue doesn't exist.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about unnecessary processing when submodules are disabled.

findings.message: this needs improvements. like referencing important files, mentioning it follows APSS starndard XXX. etc. very concise.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is feedback on a test fixture file, not production code. The file is under `tests/fixtures/dead_references/` — it exists solely to set up a test scenario for the dead reference validator. The finding is also phrased as personal preference ('needs improvements', 'very concise') with a typo ('starndard') and no specific actionable requirement. It cannot be verified as a factual code issue.
findings.severity_justification: Even if valid, this concerns a test fixture file with no user-facing impact.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about the content of a markdown context file in a test fixture.

findings.message: don't use magic strings. Should come from a central config so it can be easily promoted
findings.tp_fp_justification: Line 233 contains `let slug = standard.unwrap_or_default()` — no magic strings. The finding is terse and vague, doesn't identify which specific strings are problematic, and the PR already introduces `all_standards()` as a central registry explicitly to eliminate magic strings. The comment is unactionable as written.
findings.severity_justification: The finding doesn't identify a concrete problem.
findings.category_justification: The concern is about hardcoded string literals vs. centralized constants.

findings.message: magic string agagin
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is a terse, informal comment with a typo ('agagin') that doesn't specify which string at line 697 is problematic or why. It provides no actionable detail. Even if a magic string were present, this comment fails the non-trivial threshold — it's the same generic 'avoid magic strings' admonition as finding 28, applied without identifying the specific string or explaining the concrete risk.
findings.severity_justification: No specific issue is identified.
findings.category_justification: The concern would be about hardcoded string literals.

findings.message: I would say consistency, process but also a standrad which enables automated validation and generatation tools and other power things like a standard to be able to vectorize any directory and more.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is informal, opinion-based commentary on documentation wording with multiple typos ('standrad', 'generatation'). It expresses a personal preference about how to describe the standard's category without identifying a factual error. It cannot be objectively verified as correct or incorrect, and is not actionable as a code review finding.
findings.severity_justification: Concerns documentation wording in an overview file with no functional impact.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about the phrasing of a documentation overview file.

findings.message: this doesn't follow the claude code skills format. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding references an external URL that cannot be verified and appears to be fabricated (`code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md` is not a known Anthropic documentation endpoint). Without access to the referenced format specification, the claim that the file 'doesn't follow the format' is unverifiable. The finding provides no concrete description of what is wrong.
findings.severity_justification: Even if the format concern were valid, this is a documentation file for agent skills with no functional impact.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns the format/structure of a documentation file for agent capabilities.

findings.message: prefer human readable codes. "ADR01-dir-not-found"
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is a personal style preference about error code naming conventions ('ADR01-001' vs 'ADR01-dir-not-found') with no factual basis. The existing numeric codes are a deliberate design choice consistent with how other error codes are defined in the codebase (e.g., HTTP status codes, compiler error codes). The finding doesn't identify a bug, inconsistency with established conventions, or user-facing problem — it's purely a naming preference.
findings.severity_justification: Error code naming style has no functional impact.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about naming conventions for error codes.

findings.message: backlinking is ALWAYS apart of the standard. That's a given and sould be noted.
findings.tp_fp_justification: This is an informal opinion about how backlinking should be described in the spec, with a typo ('sould'). It contradicts the actual design: `backlinking` is explicitly configurable in the codebase (`docs.adr.backlinking = true/false` in config.rs), so 'always part of the standard' is factually incorrect per the implementation. The finding is a personal preference about documentation framing with no actionable code change.
findings.severity_justification: Concerns documentation phrasing in a spec file with no functional impact.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about how a feature is described in the specification document.

findings.message: Start with XXX, but can support up to XXXXX so regexes MUST support that flexibiliy in case ADRs grow over 1000 far away in the future
findings.tp_fp_justification: The concern is already addressed. The `ADR_STEM_PATTERN` is `\d{3,5}`, supporting 3-5 digit numbers (001-99999), which covers projects with over 1000 ADRs. The finding suggests adding flexibility that already exists in the implementation. The spec text uses `ADR-XXX` as a shorthand example, not as a constraint limiting it to 3 digits.
findings.severity_justification: The described limitation doesn't exist in the codebase.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about the spec description vs. implementation, with the implementation already being correct.

findings.message: defaults is <project-root>/docs/adrs

No factual error exists — the config table comment 'ADR directory name under docs root' correctly describes the field as a relative directory name, not the full path.

findings.category_justification: The finding is about the completeness of a configuration example comment in a spec document.

findings.category_justification: The finding questions whether a feature toggle should exist in the public configuration interface.

findings.message: Front matter parse failures and missing front matter are silently converted to `None` here and then indexed using the filename with an empty description. I couldn't find any parent-standard validation that reports missing or malformed front matter, so documents without the required metadata still pass validation despite the PR's stated goal of enforcing YAML front matter on every Markdown file.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: index.rs lines 56-58 use `.ok().flatten()` to silently drop both I/O errors and missing frontmatter, and the entire `DocValidator::validate()` call chain (readme::validate_readmes, context::validate_root_context) has no per-file frontmatter validation pass. Documents without frontmatter generate fallback entries and pass all checks. The PR description explicitly claims frontmatter is enforced on every file, but no diagnostic exists for it.
findings.severity_justification: The enforcement gap means the standard's primary stated value proposition (frontmatter-driven, machine-readable docs) cannot be verified by the validator — a project could have zero frontmatter and pass all checks. This is a meaningful functional gap, not a cosmetic issue.
findings.category_justification: The validator's behavior contradicts the documented and stated intent of the standard — it claims to enforce frontmatter but doesn't.

findings.message: The generated Markdown table inserts front matter values directly into table cells. A document name or description containing `|` or a newline will corrupt the README index table and then make validation compare against malformed generated output. Escape or normalize Markdown table cell content before rendering it.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: render_index_table at lines 103-105 (and the custom-fields path) interpolates entry.name and entry.description directly into Markdown table cells via format! with no escaping. A pipe character in a frontmatter value would split the cell, corrupting the table structure. A newline would produce extra rows. The validation path then compares README content against this generated-but-malformed output, so the corruption affects both generation and validation.
findings.severity_justification: The scenario requires a frontmatter value that contains '|' or a newline, which is unusual in practice for name/description fields. The impact (malformed README index) is real but confined to documentation output. No data loss or security risk; the worst case is a broken index table in a README.
findings.category_justification: Unescaped special characters in rendered Markdown table cells is a correctness bug — the output is structurally invalid Markdown under inputs the code doesn't guard against.

findings.message: `write_indexes` only checks `docs.index.auto_generate`, so `aps run docs index --write` will still modify README files when the docs standard is disabled (`docs.enabled = false`) or index enforcement is disabled (`docs.index.enabled = false`). The config describes `docs.enabled` as the master switch and `docs.index.enabled` as controlling README indexes, so the write path should honor those flags before making changes.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: write_indexes at lines 113-116 only checks docs.index.auto_generate before writing. It does not check docs.enabled (documented as master switch) or docs.index.enabled. validate() and validate_readmes both respect those flags, making write_indexes behaviorally inconsistent — it will mutate README files even when the feature is supposed to be disabled.
findings.severity_justification: Unexpected file mutations that bypass a documented master switch are a real correctness problem. A user who sets docs.enabled = false to suppress all docs-standard behavior would still have their README files rewritten if they run 'aps run docs index --write', violating the documented contract of the config.
findings.category_justification: The write path ignores config flags that are supposed to control whether the feature is active, contradicting the documented behavior of those flags.
